title: Compression on the web: Huffman, LZ77, Brotli, and the base64 tax
description: Compression is the cheapest speed win on the web, and it's often applied to the wrong bytes. Learn what makes data compressible, how Huffman coding and LZ77 work, why Brotli beats gzip on text, and why inlining a file as base64 makes it a third bigger.

questions.title: What does a compression algorithm exploit to shrink data?

options.text: Redundancy: repeated patterns, uneven symbol frequencies, or correlations between parts of the data.
High entropy: the more unpredictable the bytes, the more there is to shrink.
Whether the data is text or binary.
Whether the data is already encrypted.

questions.explanation: Every general-purpose compressor, from Huffman to LZ77 to Brotli, works by finding *structure*: symbols that repeat, sequences that recur, or a probability distribution that isn't flat. That structure lets it replace something long and predictable with something short. High-entropy data has no pattern left to exploit, which is why encrypted or already-compressed data barely shrinks. Text versus binary doesn't matter. Many binary formats are highly structured and compress well, while text like a list of random UUIDs barely compresses.

questions.title: Why does gzipping a file that's already `.gz` usually make it slightly *bigger*?

options.text: The first pass already removed the structure, so the output looks almost random to the second pass. The second gzip wrapper then adds its own header and checksum.
gzip has a bug that lets it compress a file only once.
Compressing twice always halves the size again, which rounds up to a bigger file for small inputs.
The operating system pads any file with a `.gz` extension.

questions.explanation: Well-compressed output has no redundancy or uneven byte frequencies left, so to a second compressor it looks like random noise. gzip can't shrink noise, but the outer gzip wrapper still adds its fixed header, flags, and CRC-32 trailer. You end up with a few extra bytes and no savings. The same fact makes compressing encrypted data pointless, as a later Question shows.

questions.title: The pigeonhole principle and lossless compression

options.text: There are more possible N-bit inputs than strings shorter than N bits, so not every N-bit input can map to a shorter output.
So no lossless compressor can shrink every possible input. Some inputs must stay the same size or grow.
A clever enough general-purpose algorithm could still save at least 1 bit on every input, even truly random data.
That's why real compressors store an incompressible chunk as-is with a small marker instead of promising to always shrink it.

questions.explanation: It comes down to counting. There are 2ⁿ distinct N-bit inputs but only 2ⁿ − 1 strings shorter than N bits (all the strings from 0 to N−1 bits combined). A lossless compressor must be reversible, so each short output can stand for only one input. That leaves at least one N-bit input with no shorter output available. The argument applies to every lossless scheme, which is why gzip and Brotli include an uncompressed 'stored' block type for data that won't shrink.

questions.title: You need to gzip and encrypt a payload before sending it. Which comes first?

options.text: Compress, then encrypt. Compression needs structure, and good ciphertext has none.
Encrypt, then compress. Compression works better on random-looking encrypted bytes.
The order makes no measurable difference.
Do both at once in a single combined cipher-and-compressor pass.

questions.explanation: Good ciphertext is designed to look like random noise. Compress it afterward and there's no structure left, so you spend CPU for nothing. Compress the plaintext while it still has redundancy, then encrypt the smaller result. One caveat, covered later in this quiz: if a response mixes a *secret* with *attacker-controlled* input, compressing it can leak the secret through the response length, even when it's encrypted afterward. That's how the BREACH and CRIME attacks work.

questions.title: What should decide whether you export an image as lossless or lossy?
questions.description: A photo tool offers a lossless (PNG-like) master export and a lossy (JPEG-like) web export of the same image.

options.text: What the next consumer needs. An archival master must survive future edits, while a web thumbnail can lose invisible detail in exchange for a much smaller file.
Always pick whichever format produces the smaller file.
Lossless is objectively better quality, so prefer it whenever storage allows.
The content decides: photographs must always be stored lossy.

questions.explanation: The same image can be stored either way, so the choice depends on what happens to the bytes next. An archival master, or an image you'll keep editing, needs every pixel preserved (lossless). A thumbnail shown once on a phone screen can drop detail nobody will notice and download much faster (lossy). Picking the smallest file ignores that lossy compression throws information away for good. That's fine for some uses and unacceptable for others, like a RAW photo, a medical scan, or source code. And photos are often stored losslessly, as RAW or PNG, when fidelity matters more than size.

questions.title: With these symbol frequencies (out of 100), which symbol gets the shortest Huffman codeword?

images.alt: Bar chart of six symbol frequencies out of 100: a is 45, d is 16, b is 13, c is 12, e is 9, f is 5

options.text: `a`, because it appears far more often than any other symbol.
`f`, because the rarest symbol always gets the shortest code to leave room for the common ones.
All six get the same length, because Huffman codes are fixed-length.
`d`, because the middle frequency gets the shortest code.

questions.explanation: Huffman coding builds its tree bottom-up by repeatedly merging the two *least* frequent nodes. Rare symbols end up deep in the tree, and frequent ones stay near the root with fewer bits. `a` makes up 45 of the 100 symbols, so it gets a 1-bit codeword (`0`), while `f`, with 5, ends up 4 bits deep. Spending fewer bits on common symbols and more on rare ones brings the average length per symbol below what any fixed-length code can reach.

questions.title: What's the shortest total length, in bits, of this 100-symbol message under an optimal Huffman code?
questions.description: Frequencies: `a`=45, `b`=13, `c`=12, `d`=16, `e`=9, `f`=5 (100 symbols total). Build the Huffman tree, read off each symbol's codeword length, then add up frequency × codeword length for all six symbols.

images.alt: Bar chart of six symbol frequencies out of 100: a is 45, d is 16, b is 13, c is 12, e is 9, f is 5
Huffman tree built from the six frequencies, showing every merge step and the resulting codeword for each leaf

questions.explanation: Merge the two smallest nodes each time: `f`(5)+`e`(9)→14, `c`(12)+`b`(13)→25, `d`(16)+14→30, 25+30→55, then `a`(45)+55→100. That gives these codeword lengths: `a` is 1 bit, `b`, `c`, and `d` are 3 bits, and `e` and `f` are 4 bits. The total is (45×1) + (13×3) + (12×3) + (16×3) + (9×4) + (5×4) = 45 + 39 + 36 + 48 + 36 + 20 = **224 bits**. The smallest fixed-length code for six symbols needs 3 bits each, or 300 bits. The saving of about 25% comes from giving `a`, almost half the message, a single bit.

questions.title: Why must Huffman codewords be prefix-free (no codeword is the start of another)?

options.text: The decoder can read bits left to right and know the moment a codeword is complete, with no separators or lookahead.
It makes every codeword the same length.
It's a legal requirement for compression formats, not a technical one.
It lets the encoder run in constant time regardless of input size.

questions.explanation: With a prefix-free code, once the bits read so far match a codeword, no longer codeword can start with those same bits. The decoder never has to peek ahead or look for separators. It walks the tree bit by bit until it reaches a leaf, outputs that symbol, and starts again at the root. Variable-length codes depend on this property. Without it, decoding needs lookahead and can even become ambiguous, as the next Question shows.

questions.title: What goes wrong when a code isn't prefix-free?
questions.description: A broken code assigns `0` to symbol A and `01` to symbol B. Because `01` starts with A's codeword `0`, the code isn't prefix-free. The diagram shows a decoder trying to read the bitstream `010`.

images.alt: The bitstream 010 decoded two ways under a non-prefix-free code: taking A first gets stuck on a leftover 10, while waiting for B first parses as B then A

options.text: After reading `0`, the decoder can't tell whether it has A or the start of B. Taking A leaves `10`, which matches nothing; only reading B (`01`) and then A (`0`) works. The bits alone don't say where codewords end.
Nothing breaks: any variable-length code can be decoded left to right with no lookahead, prefix-free or not.
The bitstream ends up exactly one bit longer than it needs to be.
It only becomes a problem once codewords are longer than four bits.

questions.explanation: `01` is `0` with one more bit, so a decoder reading `010` hits a fork after the first `0`. It has already matched A, but B might be coming. If it commits to A, it's left with `10`, which isn't a codeword. To decode correctly, it has to look ahead or back up and try B (`01`) followed by A (`0`). With a slightly bigger code, things get worse: add C = `10`, and `010` is both B A and A C, with nothing in the bits to say which the encoder meant. Prefix-free codes rule this out, and Huffman's tree construction always produces one. It's a correctness requirement.

questions.title: A symbol appears 99% of the time. Why can't Huffman coding spend less than 1 bit on it, and what can?

options.text: Huffman codewords are whole numbers of bits, so 1 bit is the minimum. Arithmetic (or range) coding can spend a *fraction* of a bit per symbol and get much closer to the entropy limit.
Huffman can't handle probabilities above 90%, and nothing can compress such data further.
Add more symbols to the alphabet until the frequencies even out.
Raise the compressor's compression level.

questions.explanation: A symbol with probability 0.99 carries only about 0.014 bits of information (−log₂ 0.99), so an ideal coder would spend far less than 1 bit on it. A Huffman tree has binary branches, so every codeword is a whole number of bits, and 1 bit per occurrence is the best Huffman can do however skewed the data is. Arithmetic coding, and its relative range coding, avoid this by encoding the whole message as one high-precision number, so a very common symbol can cost well under a bit on average. That's why formats chasing the best ratio, like the HEVC and AV1 video codecs, use arithmetic or range coding instead of Huffman, or alongside it.

questions.title: Static versus dynamic Huffman tables
questions.description: A compressor can use a fixed Huffman table agreed on in advance, or build a new one from each file's actual symbol frequencies. Select every correct statement.

options.text: A dynamic table fits the file's real symbol frequencies, so it can compress better than a generic static table.
A dynamic table has to be stored with the compressed data, which adds overhead a static table avoids.
On a very small file, storing a dynamic table can cost more than it saves.
A static table has to be rebuilt and sent with every file, just like a dynamic one.

questions.explanation: A dynamic table (DEFLATE builds one per block) matches the data's exact frequencies. But the decoder needs the same table, so the table travels with the compressed bytes and its size comes out of the savings. On a tiny file, that cost can eat most or all of the benefit. A static table is agreed on in advance, built into the format or negotiated, so it costs nothing per file. The downside is that it's tuned for typical data, not your file. The false statement has it backwards: not resending the table is the whole point of a static one.

questions.title: LZ77 replaces a repeated run of bytes with a back-reference. What do the numbers in a `(distance, length)` pair mean?

images.alt: A sliding window of already-seen bytes, a lookahead buffer of upcoming bytes, and an arrow showing a back-reference matching earlier data

options.text: `distance` is how many bytes back in the output the match starts; `length` is how many bytes to copy from there.
`distance` is how many bytes to skip ahead in the output; `length` is the size of the sliding window.
`distance` is the offset from the start of the file; `length` is how many matches have been found so far.
They're two unrelated Huffman codeword lengths.

questions.explanation: LZ77 keeps a sliding window of recent output and looks for the upcoming bytes inside it. When it finds a match, it emits a short token instead of the bytes: go back `distance` bytes and copy `length` bytes. The decoder has already produced everything in the window, so it can repeat the copy exactly. Distance is measured from the current position, not the start of the file. The window moves forward as decoding goes on, and a back-reference can only reach what's inside it.

questions.title: An LZ77-based compressor has a 32 KiB sliding window. What's the largest `distance`, in bytes, a back-reference can reach?
questions.explanation: 32 KiB = 32 × 1024 = **32,768 bytes**. That's the hard limit on how far back a match can reach, and DEFLATE (used by gzip and zlib) uses exactly this window size. Anything repeated within the last 32,768 bytes can become a cheap back-reference. Anything that last appeared further back is invisible to the matcher and gets encoded again from scratch. Files that repeat content over long distances, like big logs or a large HTML page with repeated blocks far apart, benefit from bigger windows. That's why Brotli and zstd support windows much larger than DEFLATE's 32 KiB.

questions.title: Encoding `abcabcabcabc` by hand: how many back-reference tokens do you need?
questions.description: The 12-character string starts with the first `abc` as three literal characters, since there's nothing earlier to reference. Each of the remaining three `abc` repetitions becomes one `(distance=3, length=3)` token. How many back-reference tokens cover the remaining 9 characters?
questions.explanation: The first `abc` (characters 1 to 3) has to be stored as literals because there's nothing earlier to point to. The remaining 9 characters are three more copies of `abc`, and one `(distance=3, length=3)` token per copy makes **3 tokens**. A smarter encoder can do it with one. LZ77 copies byte by byte, so a length can be longer than its distance: a single `(distance=3, length=9)` token copies `abc`, then copies the `abc` it just wrote, and so on, covering all 9 characters. DEFLATE and similar formats support these overlapping copies.

questions.title: DEFLATE runs LZ77 first, then Huffman coding. What kind of redundancy does each stage catch?

images.alt: Pipeline diagram showing raw data entering an LZ77 stage that outputs literals and back-references, then a Huffman stage that entropy-codes the result

options.text: LZ77 catches repeated substrings with back-references; Huffman then catches uneven frequencies in what's left (the literals and back-reference codes).
Huffman catches repeated substrings; LZ77 catches uneven symbol frequencies.
Both stages catch the same redundancy; the second pass is only a safety margin.
LZ77 only handles text, and Huffman only handles binary data.

questions.explanation: The stages complement each other. LZ77 runs first and finds repeated sequences, replacing repeats with short back-reference tokens. Its output is a stream of literal bytes and tokens whose values are unevenly distributed: some literals, lengths, and distances show up much more often than others. Huffman coding then gives the most common ones shorter codewords, catching frequency skew that substring matching can't see. Either stage alone does worse. LZ77 alone leaves that uneven token stream, and Huffman alone misses repeated multi-byte sequences.

questions.title: gzip, zlib, and raw deflate all use the same DEFLATE algorithm. Select every correct statement about how they differ.

options.text: gzip wraps the DEFLATE stream in its own header and a CRC-32 checksum trailer. It's the format behind HTTP's `Content-Encoding: gzip`.
zlib wraps the same stream in a smaller header and an Adler-32 checksum, and appears inside formats like PNG.
Raw deflate is just the bitstream, with no header or checksum. It's used when an outer container, like a ZIP entry, already provides that framing.
The three formats use incompatible algorithms, and each needs a completely different decompressor for the compressed data.

questions.explanation: All three run the same DEFLATE algorithm; they differ only in the wrapper. gzip (RFC 1952) adds a header, with fields like a filename and timestamp, and a CRC-32 trailer for integrity checks. It's what a server sends with `Content-Encoding: gzip`. zlib (RFC 1950) is a thinner wrapper, a 2-byte header plus a 4-byte Adler-32 checksum, used inside PNG images and Git objects. Raw deflate (RFC 1951) is the bare bitstream, used when the outer format (like a `.zip` file's per-entry metadata) already tracks sizes and checksums. A decompressor only has to know which wrapper bytes to strip first.

questions.title: Choosing a gzip compression level: 6 versus 9
questions.description: Select every correct statement about how size and time change as the compression level goes up.

images.alt: Chart of compressed size and compression time plotted against gzip level 1 through 9, showing size dropping sharply at first then flattening while time keeps climbing

options.text: Level 9 usually saves only a little more than level 6, but takes much longer to compress.
Static assets compressed once at build time and served from cache many times can justify level 9.
Dynamic responses compressed on every request usually do better with a faster level like 6, because compression time adds directly to response time.
Level 9 also decompresses noticeably slower for the client, which is the main reason to avoid it.

questions.explanation: Returns drop off fast. Going from level 1 to 6 gets most of the possible savings. Level 9 usually trims only a few more percent, while the encoder's search effort, and its time, keeps climbing. That's why one build pipeline can use different levels in different places. An asset built once and served from a CDN for months can afford a slow, maximum-ratio step. An API response generated on every request needs fast compression, because that time adds to the response latency. The false statement confuses encoding with decoding. DEFLATE decompresses at about the same speed whatever level produced the data, so slow *encoding* is why high levels are skipped on hot paths.

questions.title: Brotli ships with a large built-in dictionary of common web text. Why does that help it beat gzip on small HTML, CSS, and JS files?

options.text: Brotli can reference common web strings it already knows, even in a tiny file with little repetition of its own. gzip's LZ77 window can't do that, because it only looks back within the file being compressed.
The dictionary makes Brotli compress faster, not smaller.
Brotli's dictionary only applies to images, not text.
gzip actually beats Brotli on small files; the dictionary only matters for streaming video.

questions.explanation: Brotli's built-in dictionary holds common strings taken from real web content: HTML tags, CSS property names, JavaScript keywords, and frequent English words and phrases. A small file doesn't have much room to repeat itself, and gzip can only match against bytes it has already seen in that same file, so it has little to work with. Brotli can match against its dictionary from the first byte, as if it had already read a lot of typical web text. That's why its lead over gzip is largest on small, boilerplate-heavy text files.

questions.title: Why does Brotli's lead over gzip shrink on a large, unique payload, like a big proprietary binary file?

options.text: The built-in dictionary is tuned for web text, which a large unique payload barely contains. Both compressors then rely mostly on the file's own redundancy, where they perform much more alike.
Brotli turns off its dictionary above a fixed file size.
Large files can't be entropy-coded with Huffman-style methods.
gzip gets a larger sliding window than Brotli once files pass a certain size.

questions.explanation: Brotli's dictionary is fixed and built from typical web content, so it only helps when the input looks like that. A large, unique binary file mostly doesn't, so Brotli falls back on the same kind of within-file LZ77 plus entropy coding that gzip uses. Brotli still has a larger match window and somewhat better entropy coding, so it can stay a bit ahead. The big win on small HTML, CSS, and JS comes from the dictionary, though, and a large payload unlike web text doesn't get it.

questions.title: Brotli quality levels: when is the highest one worth it?
questions.description: Brotli has quality levels, much like gzip's compression levels, but its top levels are far slower to *encode*. Select every correct statement.

options.text: Quality 11 (the maximum) makes sense for static assets compressed once at build time and then served from cache.
Dynamic responses compressed on every request should use a much lower quality, because compression time adds directly to response time.
Using quality 11 for a one-time build artifact costs nothing at request time. It only makes the build longer.
Higher quality levels also make decoding noticeably slower in the browser.

questions.explanation: Brotli's quality setting mostly changes *encoding* effort: how hard the compressor searches for matches and builds its tables. Decoding stays fast at any quality. So a site can use two settings. Assets built once and served unchanged for months can take quality 11's long compression time, because that cost is paid once, offline, and never during a request. A dynamic response is compressed on every request, so a slow quality-11 encode would add latency to every page load. That's why servers compressing on the fly usually pick a much lower quality.

questions.title: Where does zstd usually sit on the speed/ratio curve compared with gzip and Brotli/xz?

options.text: At similar settings, zstd is usually much faster than gzip and compresses as well or better.
At its highest levels, zstd's ratio can approach Brotli/xz, though not always match it, while still decompressing very fast.
zstd has a wide range of levels, so you can trade speed for ratio much like gzip's level setting.
zstd gets its speed by being lossy, unlike gzip and Brotli.

questions.explanation: zstd was designed to get a better speed/ratio trade-off than older tools. At its default and lower levels, it compresses and decompresses much faster than gzip with similar or better ratios, which is why it's popular for hot paths like log storage and network protocols. At its highest levels, it gives up some speed to reach ratios near Brotli or xz, without fully matching their best results, and decompression stays fast at every level. zstd is lossless, like gzip and Brotli: all of them restore the exact original bytes.

questions.title: A company serves thousands of small, similar JSON API responses and trains a *custom* compression dictionary on its past traffic. What's the idea?

options.text: It's Brotli's built-in dictionary trick applied to your own data. The compressor can reference patterns common across your payloads, even when a single response is too small to repeat much on its own.
Custom dictionaries only work for image formats, not structured text like JSON.
A shared dictionary replaces Huffman and other entropy coding with a plain lookup table.
Custom dictionaries make each response bigger in exchange for faster generation.

questions.explanation: A custom dictionary works like Brotli's built-in one, but it's built from a sample of *your* traffic instead of general web text: repeated JSON keys, boilerplate structure, and common field values. The compressor can reference that shared context from the first byte of a new, tiny response. Concatenating small files before gzipping them, covered later in this quiz, uses the same idea. Small payloads compress poorly alone because they don't repeat much internally, but they often repeat a lot *across* each other. A shared dictionary, or a shared file, lets the compressor use that.

questions.title: A browser sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br` and gets a response with `Content-Encoding: br`. What does each header do?

options.text: `Accept-Encoding` (on the request) lists the encodings the client can decode; `Content-Encoding` (on the response) says which one the server used for this body.
They mean the same thing; one just appears on requests and the other on responses.
`Accept-Encoding` picks the encoding; `Content-Encoding` only matters for image responses.
`Content-Encoding` on a response tells the browser to compress its *next* request the same way.

questions.explanation: The two headers are a negotiation. `Accept-Encoding` tells the server what the client can decode, and the server can pick any encoding from that list or none at all (identity). `Content-Encoding` then states what was actually done to this body: it was compressed with gzip, br, or similar, and the client must decode it before reading it as its media type. People often mix these up, especially once `Transfer-Encoding` joins in (the next Question). All three have 'Encoding' in the name but handle different things.

questions.title: How does `Transfer-Encoding` differ from `Content-Encoding`?

images.alt: One HTTP response with Content-Encoding and Transfer-Encoding headers highlighted, each pointing at a different layer the header belongs to

options.text: `Transfer-Encoding` (like `chunked`) describes how the body is framed for one hop over the wire, and the receiver strips it before passing the payload on. `Content-Encoding` (like `gzip`) belongs to the payload itself, end to end, and the final consumer decodes it.
`Transfer-Encoding` is deprecated and no longer appears in modern HTTP.
The two headers are different names for the same mechanism.
`Transfer-Encoding` only applies to requests, never responses.

questions.explanation: The difference is *hop-by-hop* versus *end-to-end*. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` describes how the body is split into pieces on one connection. A proxy can un-chunk it and re-chunk it differently, and the chunking is gone by the time the body reaches the application. It's wire framing, not content. `Content-Encoding: gzip` travels unchanged to the final consumer. A proxy must not quietly strip it, because the receiving application expects to decode the payload itself. `Transfer-Encoding` is still common in HTTP/1.1, where chunked transfer is the standard way to stream a response of unknown length, and both headers can appear on the same response, each working at its own layer.

questions.title: A server returns different bodies for the same URL based on `Accept-Encoding` but leaves out `Vary: Accept-Encoding`. What can go wrong?

options.text: A shared cache (a CDN or proxy) may store the response under the URL alone, then serve the gzip-compressed bytes to a client that sent no `Accept-Encoding` and can't read them.
Nothing much; `Vary` only affects server access logs.
Browsers refuse to render any page served through a cache that lacks `Vary`.
Without `Vary`, the server stops compressing responses for that URL for good.

questions.explanation: A shared cache normally uses the URL as the cache key and assumes every client gets the same response. That breaks when one URL produces different bytes depending on a request header, as it does when the server picks gzip, br, or no encoding based on `Accept-Encoding`. `Vary: Accept-Encoding` tells the cache to include that header in the key, so compressed and uncompressed versions are stored as separate entries. Without it, a cache can hand one client bytes encoded for another, like compressed data to a client that never asked for compression. This bug shows up in real deployments.

questions.title: For which of these does adding gzip or Brotli on top waste CPU for close to 0% extra savings?
questions.description: Select every format where this is true.

options.text: A JPEG photo
A WebP image
An MP4 video
A hand-written CSS stylesheet

questions.explanation: JPEG, WebP, and MP4 are already the output of specialized compressors. Their encoders have removed most of the redundancy using techniques like transform coding, motion prediction, and entropy coding tuned to image, video, and audio data, which go far beyond what a general byte-level compressor does. gzip or Brotli finds almost no structure left, the same problem as compressing compressed data covered earlier, so the server spends CPU for a tiny change in size, or sometimes a slightly bigger file. Plain text like CSS is what general-purpose compression is built for: repeated tokens, whitespace, and uneven character frequencies.

questions.title: Why do most servers skip compressing very small responses, say under about 1 KB?

options.text: The format's own overhead (headers, tables, checksums) plus the CPU cost can cancel out the savings on something that small, and the result is sometimes bigger than the original.
Small responses are already implicitly encrypted, so compression is redundant.
HTTP forbids `Content-Encoding` on responses under 1 KB.
Browsers ignore `Content-Encoding` on responses that small.

questions.explanation: Every compression format has a fixed cost regardless of payload size: a header, maybe a checksum, and for DEFLATE, possibly a Huffman table. On a large payload that cost is negligible. On a response of a few hundred bytes, it's a real fraction of the size and can make the output bigger than the input, after spending CPU to produce it. Servers and CDNs set a minimum size to avoid this. HTTP itself has no such rule, and browsers decode compressed responses of any size.

questions.title: A response mixes a secret token with attacker-controlled input and is compressed before being sent over HTTPS. What does the compressed length leak?
questions.description: This is the setup behind the BREACH and CRIME attacks.

images.alt: Chart of compressed response length across a series of attacker guesses, showing a visible dip in length exactly when a guess matches part of the hidden secret

options.text: When the attacker's guess matches part of the secret, the compressor replaces the overlap with a cheap back-reference and the response gets measurably shorter. By repeating guesses and watching the length, the attacker recovers the secret byte by byte.
Compression exposes the encryption key as bytes in the compressed output.
The attack works even when the attacker can't influence any part of the response body.
It only affects plain HTTP; HTTPS responses are immune.

questions.explanation: The attack never breaks the encryption. It uses what compression does before encryption runs. Say a response contains a secret, like a CSRF token, and text the attacker controls, like a reflected query parameter. The attacker requests the page many times with different guesses in their input. When a guess matches part of the secret, the compressor encodes the overlap as a back-reference and the compressed response gets shorter. TLS hides content but not size, so the attacker can see that. Trying one character at a time and watching for the drop, they rebuild the secret without decrypting anything. The attack needs *both* a secret and attacker-controlled content in the same compressed response, which is what the defenses in the next Question target.

questions.title: What's the standard defense against BREACH and CRIME-style compression attacks?

options.text: Don't compress responses that mix a secret with attacker-influenced content. Keep secrets away from reflected input, turn off compression for those responses, or add random padding or masking so the length no longer tracks the secret.
Switch from gzip to Brotli, which is immune to this kind of attack.
Use a longer TLS key.
Turn off HTTPS and serve the page over plain HTTP.

questions.explanation: The weakness is the situation, not the algorithm: a secret and attacker-controlled content share one compressed, encrypted response, and the attacker can see its length. The fix has to change that situation. Don't put secrets and untrusted input in the same compressed response, turn off compression for responses carrying sensitive tokens, randomize secret tokens per request so a partial match doesn't carry over, or add random padding so the length doesn't reveal the secret. Brotli uses back-references just like gzip, so switching doesn't help. A longer TLS key doesn't help either, because the leak happens in compression before encryption, and dropping HTTPS would only make things much worse.

questions.title: A binary file is exactly 300,000 bytes. About how many bytes is its base64 text, ignoring padding?
questions.description: Base64 turns every 3 input bytes into 4 output characters of 1 byte each.

images.alt: Three input bytes, 24 bits total, split into four 6-bit groups, each mapped to one base64 output character

questions.explanation: 300,000 bytes is exactly 100,000 groups of 3 bytes, and each group becomes 4 characters: 100,000 × 4 = **400,000 bytes**, 33% larger than the original. No padding is needed because 300,000 divides evenly by 3. The 33% comes from using only 64 printable ASCII characters, which carry 6 bits each: 3 bytes (24 bits) become 4 characters of 6 bits. Every base64 payload pays this ratio.

questions.title: When does inlining an image as a base64 data URI help performance, and when does it hurt?
questions.description: A 2 KB SVG icon is embedded in the HTML as a base64 data URI instead of linked as a separate file.

options.text: It can help for one tiny, critical, above-the-fold asset by saving a network round trip. It hurts for assets used across pages, since the roughly 33% base64 overhead repeats in every response and the asset loses its own browser cache entry.
It always helps, because base64 text compresses better than the original binary.
It always hurts and should never be used.
The trade-off only matters for assets larger than 1 MB.

questions.explanation: Inlining swaps one cost, an extra request, for another, a bigger HTML document that caches less well. Which wins depends on the case. A small, critical asset needed right away, like an above-the-fold icon that would otherwise wait on its own request, can benefit, because saving the round trip matters more than the base64 overhead. An asset used on many pages loses out. Instead of downloading once and then coming from the browser cache, its larger base64 form is downloaded again inside every HTML page that uses it. The base64 overhead applies at any size, not only to large files.

questions.title: A CSS file embeds a large image as a base64 `data:` URI in a `background-image` rule. What's the downside of putting it in CSS instead of HTML?

options.text: The browser can't apply any rule in that stylesheet, even ones unrelated to the image, until the whole file, base64 data included, has downloaded and been parsed. One embedded image can delay all the styles.
CSS can't contain `data:` URIs, so the page breaks.
Embedding the image this way makes it render at the wrong resolution.
It turns off gzip/Brotli compression for the rest of the file.

questions.explanation: CSS blocks rendering: the browser doesn't paint until it has the full stylesheet, because a later rule could override an earlier one. That's usually fine, since CSS files tend to be small. A large base64 image makes the blocking file much bigger, so every unrelated rule (layout, typography, colors) waits for the image data to download and parse. A normal image URL loads separately and doesn't hold up the CSS. The `data:` syntax is valid CSS, and compression still applies to the whole file. The problem is only that the image now sits inside a render-blocking file.

questions.title: You can minify a JS file before gzipping it, or gzip the unminified original. How does minification's raw-size saving compare with its saving *after* gzip?

options.text: Minification still makes the gzipped file smaller, but by much less than the raw difference suggests. gzip already removes much of the same redundancy (whitespace, repeated tokens, long names), so their gains overlap.
Minification makes no difference once gzip runs.
Minification and gzip savings simply add up, with no overlap.
Minifying the gzipped output compresses better than minifying before gzipping.

questions.explanation: Minification and gzip go after much of the same redundancy. Whitespace and comments are cheap for gzip anyway, since repeated runs of spaces compress very well, and gzip's back-references already catch much of the repetition in long variable names. So minifying often cuts the raw file by 30 to 60%, but the gap between the minified and unminified *gzipped* files is much smaller. Minifying is still worth it: it also cuts parse and execution time, and gzip can't make identifiers shorter. Just don't estimate the gzipped benefit from the raw difference. (Minifying gzipped output makes no sense, since minifiers work on source text, not compressed bytes.)

questions.title: Why does gzipping 200 small JSON files concatenated into one beat gzipping each file separately?
questions.description: Select every statement that correctly explains the size difference.

options.text: In one stream, LZ77 can back-reference structure repeated across what used to be separate files, like shared keys and formatting.
The fixed gzip header and CRC-32 trailer are paid once instead of 200 times.
Huffman tables are built and stored for the combined data, instead of a new table for every tiny file.
gzip decompresses one concatenated file noticeably faster than 200 separate files, and that's what makes it smaller.

questions.explanation: This is the same idea as Brotli's built-in dictionary and custom shared dictionaries, both covered earlier. Small files don't repeat much internally, but they often repeat a lot across each other: the same JSON keys and the same boilerplate. A compressor can only use that repetition if the files come in one stream. Concatenating them gives LZ77 the cross-file context, lets Huffman tables cover the whole batch instead of paying for 200 of them, and replaces 200 gzip headers and trailers with one. Decompression speed has nothing to do with it, since it doesn't affect compressed size.
